summary: Defines a network management architecture that runs the ISO management services and protocol, CMIS and CMIP, in a TCP/IP environment. It provides a way for managers and managed devices to exchange control and monitoring information. It was replaced by RFC 1189.

eli5.summary: Network gear needs someone to check up on it. This describes a way to use one family of checkup rules on the Internet's own kind of network.

subtitle: A protocol for ISO network management over TCP/IP networks.

tldr.problem: SNMP was designed as a quick fix for network management. The Internet community also wanted a more powerful, standards-based approach using ISO protocols that could scale to complex networks and provide a migration path to full OSI systems.
tldr.mechanism: CMOT (CMIP Over TCP/IP) runs ISO management protocols (ACSE, ROSE, CMIP) on top of TCP and UDP instead of the full ISO stack. A lightweight presentation layer bridges the gap. Managers and agents establish associations and exchange management operations using a rich object model.
tldr.outcome: CMOT demonstrated feasibility of ISO management in TCP/IP networks, but its complexity and SNMP's simplicity meant SNMP became dominant. CMOT was replaced by RFC 1189, but influenced the future direction of network management standards.

today: RFC 1095 is a draft standard superseded by RFC 1189. CMOT demonstrated the feasibility of running ISO management protocols over TCP/IP, but SNMP's simplicity made it the dominant protocol. However, CMOT's concepts influenced later management standards, and research networks deployed experimental CMOT systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Architecture
sections.content:
RFC 1095 defines CMOT, which stands for Common Management Information Protocol Over TCP/IP. CMOT brings ISO network management standards (CMIS/CMIP) to TCP/IP environments. It addresses the longer-term needs of the Internet community for a powerful, standards-based approach that could eventually replace SNMP.

The Internet Activities Board directed three working groups: one to define the MIB, one to refine SNMP for short-term needs, and one (the Netman working group) to develop CMOT for the long term. CMOT is built on the OSI Management Framework, which provides a rich model for organizing management information and a comprehensive set of management services.
sections.eli5: While SNMP was a quick, simple solution, CMOT is a more serious, international standard for network management. It's what you'd use if you needed powerful management in a large network and wanted to follow international standards.

sections.title: The OSI Management Framework
sections.content:
CMOT is built on the OSI Management Framework, which structures management around three models. The organizational model divides networks into administrative domains, each with one or more managers. The functional model divides management into five areas: fault management (detecting and correcting problems), configuration management (changing settings), performance management (monitoring health), accounting management (charging for resource use), and security management (controlling access).

The information model describes management data using concepts from object-oriented design: managed objects represent network resources, object classes represent types of resources, and attributes represent properties of an object. Managed objects participate in containment hierarchies (an object contains other objects) and inheritance hierarchies (a subclass inherits properties from a superclass). The MIB is a conceptual repository of all management information accessible via the protocol.
sections.eli5: OSI management uses object-oriented thinking. A router is one type of object, an interface is another, a connection is a third. Each object has properties (attributes), and they're organized in hierarchies.

sections.title: The CMOT Protocol Stack
sections.content:
CMOT maps the full ISO management protocol stack onto TCP/IP. Instead of using ISO's presentation, session, and transport layers, CMOT uses a lightweight presentation protocol (LPP, defined in RFC 1085) that sits between the ISO application layer (ACSE, ROSE, CMISE) and TCP/UDP. This design reduces complexity while preserving the ability to migrate to full ISO protocols later.

The stack consists of: CMISE (Common Management Information Service Element), which provides the actual management services; ROSE (Remote Operations Service Element), which handles remote operation invocations; ACSE (Association Control Service Element), which establishes and releases associations between managers and agents; the lightweight presentation layer, which encodes and decodes ASN.1 messages; and TCP or UDP for transport. The choice between TCP (reliable, connection-oriented) and UDP (simple, connectionless) is left to the application.
sections.eli5: CMOT takes ISO management protocols and puts them on top of TCP/IP instead of ISO protocols. The lightweight presentation layer translates between the two worlds. It's like putting a European electrical device in a North American socket with an adapter.

sections.title: CMIS Services and Operations
sections.content:
CMOT defines a rich set of CMIS services for management. Association services (M-INITIALISE, M-TERMINATE, M-ABORT) manage the connection. Notification services (M-EVENT-REPORT) report asynchronous events. Operation services include M-GET (retrieve management information), M-SET (modify settings), M-ACTION (execute a remote action), M-CREATE (instantiate a new managed object), and M-DELETE (remove a managed object).

CMOT also supports scoping, filtering, and synchronization. Scoping allows a request to apply to multiple objects in a containment tree. Filtering further restricts the selection based on attribute values (e.g., all routing entries with age greater than 100). Synchronization can be "best effort" (if one fails, continue with others) or "atomic" (all succeed or all fail). These features allow a single request to operate on a collection of managed objects, reducing the number of round trips needed.
sections.eli5: CMOT has operations like "get this information", "change this setting", "run this action", or "create a new object". You can also ask to see all routing table entries matching certain conditions instead of asking for each one individually.

sections.title: Representing Internet MIB in CMOT
sections.content:
The Internet MIB was originally defined for SNMP in RFC 1066. To use it with CMOT, RFC 1095 defines how Internet SMI (Structure of Management Information) maps to ISO SMI. Internet SMI uses simple "object types" without explicit object classes; CMOT imposes an object class structure on the Internet MIB.

The mapping defines how to identify managed object instances using distinguished names (a path through the containment hierarchy). For example, an IP routing table entry is identified by the system (e.g., "gateway1") and the destination address (e.g., "10.0.0.51"). This allows CMOT to reference and operate on Internet MIB objects using ISO naming conventions, enabling seamless access to the same MIB data through either SNMP or CMOT.
sections.eli5: SNMP and CMOT use the same data (the Internet MIB), but CMOT accesses it differently. CMOT names objects using a hierarchy, like "this system, this interface, this connection", instead of just a flat list.

sections.title: Functional Unit Groups
sections.content:
To reduce code size and complexity, CMOT defines functional unit groups. A system announces which services it supports at association time. Manager groups range from Event Monitor (listens for notifications only) through Simple Manager (get and set), Controlling Manager (get, set, create, delete), to Full Manager (all operations). Agent groups have the same range. A system only needs to implement the operations required by its group.

This allows simple devices to support minimal CMOT (e.g., just event reporting), while full management systems support all operations. A pair of systems can communicate if their functional units have sufficient overlap. For example, a Monitoring Manager (which can get but not set) can work with a Simple Agent (which can get and set in confirmed mode).
sections.eli5: Different devices need different levels of management complexity. A simple router might just send alerts (event reports). A full network management station might do everything. CMOT lets each device announce what it can do.
